Spoke with Jonathan, the store manager, who will be the primary user processing EasyPay Finance transactions. He shared that the shop currently offers one competing financing option, but many customers struggle to qualify through that provider. He's hopeful EasyPay will provide a stronger approval solution for those customers. While he wasn't able to provide insight into the competitor's underwriting criteria, I reviewed our qualification requirements and approval process, which he appreciated and said gave him confidence in presenting the program to customers.

Jonathan noted that financing opportunities are relatively infrequent at this location, suggesting there is not yet a strong financing culture. Subject: 00UTO00000cRwzi2AC
Full Comments:
Checked in via Maps Application 
Spoke with Sabrina, the manager. After several months of follow-up visits encouraging the shop to use EasyPay again, they are finally back on board and are now running EasyPay first. They are once again producing the same level of business they did with us when we were RIC, which is a great win.

This is a good example of how consistent relationship-building and periodic follow-up can help re-engage inactive merchants over time.

Sabrina shared that overall business has been slower, but higher repair costs have resulted in larger average ticket sizes, helping offset the decrease in car count. Based on their current activity, I estimate they have the potential to fund approximately $8K–$10K with EasyPay each month.

The shop is currently on a $20 spiff. Sabrina requested a poster, which I will provide once they are back in stock. I reminded her to reach out to Connor or me if she needs any assistance.

Subject: 00TTO00000zKYQo2AO
Full Comments:
Spoke with Shirley for an account review. She provided additional insight into the location's business model and customer base. Shirley explained that they service both local customers and dealership partnerships; however, the dealership-related work does not typically utilize EasyPay. When individual customers bring in their personal vehicles, financing is most commonly needed for repairs of $2,000 or more, at which point EasyPay is offered.

Shirley noted that business tends to slow down around rent-payment periods, with volume increasing once that timeframe has passed. She confirmed that EasyPay is their primary financing solution. While they do have another financing option available, it is a credit card program with a more complicated process, and they find EasyPay to be a much simpler and more effective solution for their customers.

No questions or concerns were reported, and the account remains engaged with the program.

 If a customer ever replied STOP, blocked our number, or was opted out automatically, they stop getting EasyPay texts – including the application link you send at the counter. Getting them reconnected takes one quick text.

Boca shared that he honestly prefers using Snap and is comfortable with their program. Based on our conversation, he appears reluctant to promote or utilize EasyPay Finance at this time, despite the available incentives.

This will likely remain a low-impact location due to the strong preference for Snap and the lack of engagement with our financing program. I will maintain periodic contact, but expectations for meaningful production from this account should remain limited unless there is a change in ownership priorities or financing needs.

Subject: 00UTO00000dFFRh2AO
Full Comments:
Checked in via Maps Application 
I spoke with Tre, the manager. He said he really likes the program and has made EasyPay his go-to financing vendor. He prefers EasyPay over KOALAFI because we do not require him to separate parts and labor on repair orders. He explained that he only uses KOALAFI when EasyPay does not approve enough to cover the full repair.

Tre mentioned that he has had some issues in the past regarding sales tax on invoices. Connor previously reviewed the proper procedures with him. He asked me how the tax exemption works and whether the shop could get in trouble for not charging sales tax. I showed him the Georgia reseller tax ID number located in his Business Center and advised him to have the owner provide that number to their tax professional, who would know how to handle it appropriately.

Tre had no other questions or concerns. I left behind a few EasyPay pens and notepads and reminded him to reach out to Connor or me if he ever needs assistance.

Full Comments:
Called and spoke with Robert. Our conversation focused primarily on the recent application declines he has been experiencing. He shared that **EasyPay is the only financing option** they offer, so when customers are declined, they often have no alternative way to finance their repairs.

Robert provided two recent examples that have been frustrating for both him and his customers. One customer had previously completed a lease with EasyPay but was declined when applying again. Another customer was initially approved, but after the approval expired and they reapplied, the second application was denied.

Robert expressed frustration with these situations because EasyPay is their only financing solution for customers who cannot pay the full repair cost upfront. I acknowledged his concerns, thanked him for the feedback, and encouraged him to continue reaching out whenever he encounters situations where we may be able to assist.

Subject: 00UTO00000dCHQ22AO
Full Comments:
Checked in via Maps Application 
I spoke with Joe. He said everything is going well, but they haven’t had much need for financing lately.

The shop doesn’t have a dedicated front desk employee. The mechanics handle both the repairs and customer interactions, so they’re constantly moving between the shop and the office. Because of that, there’s no one specifically responsible for offering financing, and it often gets overlooked unless a customer asks about it. This has limited the number of EasyPay applications submitted.

Full Comments:
Spoke with Chris and reviewed his account activity. He shared that they still offer EasyPay whenever customers need financing, with most financed repairs ranging from $1,500 to $5,000. They also work with Landmark Finance Services; however, activity has been low with both financing options.

Chris mentioned that this location is typically very busy during the summer, but this year has been unusually slow. He said business varies from year to year, and many customers are either paying out of pocket or choosing not to move forward with repairs.

I updated the business profile and provided my contact information for future support. Chris requested that I resend the email to access the new EasyPay portal so he can complete his login setup.

EasyPay remains their go-to financing option. His only concern was the approval rate. We reviewed his dashboard and found that they had submitted eight applications, with two approvals. The positive takeaway is that they funded both approved applications, giving them an excellent pull-through rate.

I explained what I’ve been telling other shops: in the current economy, many customers are falling behind on payments, which negatively impacts their credit profiles and results in more financing declines. He understood and had no additional questions or concerns. I reminded him to reach out to Connor or me if he needs anything.

They are currently only working with EasyPay as their financial provider and are excited to begin utilizing the program. Kenny confirmed they received the marketing materials from their initial enrollment.

I advised him that I will follow up and provide my contact information for any future questions or concerns. I also let him know that Marco will be his point of contact as well.

Full Comments:
Spoke with Sam, the owner. He said business has been very challenging, with car count continuing to decline. When customers do come in for repairs, they are often only doing the bare minimum needed to keep their vehicles on the road.

Sam said he still really likes the EasyPay program but feels he has seen a lot of declines compared to Snap. I reviewed his Business Center with him and found that there have not actually been a large number of applications. From today back to July 24, he had six applications total: four were declined and two were incomplete. He showed me that two of the four EasyPay declines were ultimately approved through Snap.

Despite the declines, Sam still prefers EasyPay over Snap because we do not require him to separate parts and labor. He did not have any other callouts or concerns. He has requested a poster in the past, so I will get one to him once they are available. I reminded him to reach out if he needs any assistance.

Subject: 00TTO000011XCPc2AO
Full Comments:
Spoke with Tavon, who confirmed that Ron is the Store Manager and Garcia is the Assistant Manager. I gathered the Shop Potential details during the conversation. Tavon shared that they have three service bays and operate as a multi-store business. Their average repair order (ARO) is typically between $1,000 and $2,000, although most of their work consists of maintenance services, such as oil changes.

He explained that the shop experiences high traffic due to the volume of maintenance services they perform, seeing approximately 35 to 40 customers per day. However, because most customers' repair costs are relatively low, there is generally limited need for financing.

One customer who planned to use EasyPay had an expired approval and reapplied, but unfortunately was declined the second time and had to use the competition. JJ also ran another application this month that was declined and asked if anything had changed on our end. I explained that nothing had changed and reminded him that, given the current economic climate, more customers may be defaulting on payments or having overdrawn accounts, which can result in more declines. He understood.

Other than that, JJ had no questions or concerns. I encouraged him to reach out to Connor or me if he needs any assistance.

Called and spoke with Michael, who reached out to verify the proper steps for a recent application they processed. We reviewed the **$39 processing fee** and when it should be collected. I explained that the fee is only requested if the customer’s payment method **declines twice**. At that point, a prompt will appear on their screen instructing them to collect the $39 fee. We also reviewed that the customer can receive a **text message requesting payment of the $39 fee**.

Michael had no additional questions or concerns regarding the processing fee. I also reviewed the **minimum customer requirements**, the importance of **properly itemizing the invoice**, and the **tax exemption process**, emphasizing that taxes should not be included on the merchant invoice because EasyPay collects taxes directly from the customer.

We also reinforced the importance of **in-person verification and ensuring all transactions are completed in person**.

I encouraged Eric to continue offering financing to all customers, as you never know who may need assistance. While I was there, I also printed a QR code for him to display in the waiting area. He is fully stocked on marketing materials at this time. I reminded him to reach out to Connor or me if he needs any assistance.

Full Comments:
Spoke with Paul, the owner. He shared that he has been in the industry for 27 years and described the current slowdown as highly unusual, noting that he has been with KBC/Midas for many years and has not seen business this slow. He stated that stores across his division, spanning the lower LA area through Las Vegas, are down approximately 34% overall. He noted that the Encinitas Midas location and one or two other stores are performing more sustainably, but the majority of the division is experiencing the same decline.

Paul’s phone was ringing throughout the call, so our conversation was brief. I attempted to gather additional shop potential beyond car counts, but he was limited on time. I thanked him for his time and will revisit volume, repair order potential, and opportunities to increase EasyPay utilization on the next call. This conversation also provided helpful insight into Midas’ divisional structure and broader market performance.

Subject: Help Your Customers Get Our Texts Again
Body:
Help your customers get EasyPay texts again
 

 



If a customer stopped EasyPay texts, they can text START to 619-327-9835 to start getting them again.

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Help Your Customers Get Our Texts Again
 
 
 
 Hello,
